Health, Safety, and Asset Management
Provides critical support services to include facilities development and management;
apparatus and fleet management; logistics and supply distribution services; health, safety,
and wellness; behavioral health; and respiratory protection program management.

Human Resources
Provides human resources functions for LCFR employees, including coordination and
administration of departmental promotional examinations and management of departmental
recruitment and retention activities; assists with other workforce planning initiatives and
employee relations matters in collaboration with Loudoun County’s Department of Human
Resources (DHR); and assists the System Chief and staff in the collective bargaining and labor
relations processes.

• The FY 2027 Adopted Budget provides 13 positions to
Loudoun County Fire and Rescue (LCFR) to enable 24/7 staffing
for an ambulance and four-person staffing on the engine to the
new county-owned Philomont Fire and Rescue Station, which is
anticipated to open early FY 2028. This enhanced service level
request aligns with LCFR’s strategic goals to ensure optimal
staffing, equitable service distribution, and compliance with
national Emergency Medical Services performance standards.
• Additionally, these positions support LCFR’s recommended
service level by working toward compliance with National Fire
Protection Association 1710 standards, which call for the arrival
of fire department transport units within eight minutes or less,
thereby improving both patient outcomes and system reliability.
• This capital project was approved in the FY 2020 Capital
Improvement Plan (CIP) and includes funding to design and
construct a modern, county-owned facility to replace the
existing volunteer-owned station.
• Full-time staffing will reduce response times to align with
national standards, directly enhancing operational efficiency
and quality of service.

Overview

• The Adopted Budget provides 17 positions to increase
minimum staffing on five front-line engine companies from three
to four personnel, advancing Loudoun County Fire and
Rescue's (LCFR) compliance with National Fire Protection
Association 1710 recommendations.
• The 17 approved positions will allow LCFR to increase staffing
in five strategically located fire companies in rural western
Loudoun County: Middleburg Station 603, Hamilton Station 605,
Lucketts Station 610, and Loudoun Heights Station 626.
• The additional staffing will improve operational efficiency and
firefighter and civilian safety by allowing faster assembly across
192 square miles of rural western Loudoun County.
• This request directly implements recommendations from
significant incident reports and line-of-duty death reviews that
identified four-person engine staffing as critical to reducing risk
and improving emergency response outcomes.

Marshal III
One-time $111,556
LTF:
Recurring $702,821
LTF:

Overview

• Loudoun County Fire and Rescue (LCFR) received four
assistant fire marshal (AFM) positions to support minimum
staffing levels in the Fire Marshal’s Office (FMO). This is a
current service level request that seeks to maintain operational
safety by increasing the minimum on-duty staffing from one to
two AFMs per shift, ensuring adequate coverage for mandated
investigations and response needs.
• The FMO is staffed with two fire marshals per shift, but drops
down to one when leave is taken. The approved request will
staff the Office at three per shift, so that the FMO always
maintains a consistent minimum staffing.
• The FMO provides 24/7 emergency and non-emergency
response for incidents involving fires, explosions, hazardous
materials, and Fire Prevention Code enforcement. Increasing
staffing will reduce reliance on overtime and minimize call
stacking, which occurs when only one fire marshal is available
and there are multiple calls for service.
• Industry best practice and national safety standards
emphasize that fire investigations should be conducted by a
team of at least two personnel to ensure investigator safety and
operational effectiveness. This request supports compliance
with these standards while reducing reliance on Loudoun
County Sheriff's Office for backup.
• These activities are mandated by Virginia Code (§ 27-31
through 27-37.1) and County ordinance. Funding these positions
ensures continued ability to meet legal obligations, respond
promptly to complex incidents and maintain community safety in
the face of growing service demand.

• The Adopted Budget provides a compliance specialist
position to support the Emergency Medical Services (EMS) Cost
Recovery Program, which will be fully funded through EMS Cost
Recovery revenue. This position will ensure LCFR maintains
compliance with complex and frequently changing federal and
state regulations while maximizing ambulance billing
reimbursements from Medicare, Medicaid, and insurance
providers.
• This position will allow existing staff to continue processing
claims within three business days. Due to transport volume
growth and complexity, staff have been unable to keep up with
demand and maintain the current service level.
• Transport volume has grown by approximately 23 percent from
FY 2020 to FY 2023 (13,711 to 17,832 transports) and is
projected to exceed 21,000 transports in FY 2026, far
surpassing the capacity of the current two-person billing team.
• EMS Cost Recovery revenue has grown from $5.6 million in FY
2020 to an estimated $8.3 million in FY 2026. Sufficient revenue
exists to fund this position within the program’s administrative
cost allocation. This investment will strengthen revenue
recovery, reduce audit exposure, and ensure equitable and
accurate billing for all County residents.

General Services
The Department of General Services (DGS) operates and maintains County-owned and
leased facilities and land; acquires and manages the public safety and general vehicle fleet;
operates the Metro parking garages; and provides core internal support to all County
agencies. DGS also provides direct support to residents through the Transit, Fleet, and
Commuter Services; Public Works and Environmental Services; and Waste Management
programs. As an integral part of the County’s emergency response and recovery operations,
DGS is designated as one of the “first responders” to major County emergencies resulting
from natural or man-made disasters.

Programs
Policy, Management, and Administration
Manages mail distribution, central records, and surplus property programs countywide;
provides internal administrative support, including human resources, policy management,
financial and budget analysis, procurement functions, and coordinating DGS’s technology
infrastructure; manages the Metro parking garage contracts; and oversees the County’s
property management functions for County-owned and leased properties and facilities.

Transit, Fleet, and Commuter Services
Provides a complement of administrative oversight and operations for the County’s public
transit services provided through a contractor. Transit services include local fixed-route transit
service, including connections to Metrorail stations, paratransit service, and commuter bus
service to the greater Washington, D.C., metropolitan area. Represents the County at
regional organizations with an interest in transit services and funding, along with serving as
the Loudoun County liaison to the Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority (WMATA)
for mass transit services. Manages grant-funded programs for transit operations and capital
investments. Manages County-owned parking garages and parking operations.
Provides for the acquisition, equipping, licensing, assignment, maintenance, replacement,
and disposal of County vehicles, as well as manages vehicle replacement and maintenance.
Provides oversight of electric vehicle chargers and the compressed natural gas fueling
facility. Additionally, manages the County’s motor pool vehicles to include scheduling,
maintaining, and exchanging of vehicles.

Facility Maintenance Operations
Operates, manages, and maintains County-owned and leased facilities. Ensures necessary
replacements and upgrades to preserve the County’s assets.

Waste Management
Constructs, operates, and maintains the Loudoun County landfill, provides education and
guidance regarding the County recycling ordinance, and offers recycling opportunities for
residents and businesses.

Public Works and Environmental Services
Develops, coordinates, and delivers the County's non-regulatory energy and environmental
programs and initiatives. Supports the Loudoun County Environmental Commission, leads
the overall coordination and implementation of sustainable energy practices for the County
in support of the Energy Strategy approved by the Board of Supervisors (Board). Provides
federal and state environmental legislation review, performs environmental management
functions, and provides coordination for compliance with state and federal mandates.
Performs maintenance and inspections on stormwater facilities countywide, administers the
Loudoun County Asphalt Maintenance and Repair Program, responds to County
emergencies, maintains street name signs and certain traffic-calming measures, maintains
water and wastewater systems, and provides other essential public works functions.
Develops and implements the Stormwater Management Program, manages water and
wastewater projects, manages the County Flood Assessment and Mitigation Program, and
oversees, inspects and maintains the County owned dam infrastructure. Provides federal and
state environmental legislation review, performs environmental management functions, and
provides coordination for compliance with state and federal mandates.

maintenance staff. With these approved resources, the County

alarms), pools, elevators, fencing, doors, windows, gates, etc.

that systems continue to operate functionally and preserve
significant capital investment made by Loudoun taxpayers.

Overview

• These positions will provide direct support to operations,
ensuring the effective and efficient delivery of current service
levels across the Department of General Services.
• Internal Services – Surplus and Records Management is
experiencing an increased workload due to the rise in acquired
County facilities and staff, resulting in an increase in surplus
items received and site visits to prepare for timely and efficient
surplus removal. The support services technician will support
the maintenance of current service levels and avoid a growing
backlog. The lead courier position will help handle over 7,600
packages received annually for the Courts. This service level
has been managed using a long-term temporary staff position
since the opening of the General District Courthouse.
• Finance – The procurement assistant position (accounting
technician I) will address an increased procurement workload
due to the growth in staff within DGS and the rise in purchase
order requests, which are time-sensitive. These increases in
workload are directly related to the addition of facilities and
increased square footage, which requires maintenance. The
accounting technician II will help sustain the timely processing
of the increased number of invoices for maintenance and other
work performed to maintain and operate the County
infrastructure.
• Support – DGS staff has grown to over 200 positions, and
existing support staff cannot keep up with current requirements
related to health, safety, disciplinary actions, training, hiring,
and collective bargaining. The HR generalist will provide the HR
program manager with the necessary bandwidth to deliver
sustained support to staff and respond to critical-level actions
on time. The quality assurance specialist (new/unclassified) will
provide quality assurance/control related to janitorial services
and pest control.
• Local tax funding neutral FTE movement – This request also
reallocates the existing contract manager position from the
Metro Parking Garages Fund to the General Fund using
reallocated departmental operating budget. Originally
dedicated exclusively to Metro-related contracts, the role has
expanded to encompass a broader range of contracts that
impact the entire Department.

Health Department
The Health Department provides services that enhance and ensure the health of all Loudoun
County residents and those who work in or visit Loudoun County. The Health Department’s
community and environmental health programs offer population-based services in
collaboration with the Loudoun Health Commission, such as communicable disease
surveillance and treatment, Lyme disease mitigation initiatives, and community-based health
improvement efforts. Other services include emergency and pandemic preparedness and
response; the provision of birth and death certificates; and restaurant, swimming pool,
private well, and septic system permitting and inspections to ensure environmental and
public health protection. The Health Department also provides essential individual-based
services to women and children who would otherwise not receive medical, dental, or
nutritional evaluation and care. The Health Department transitioned from a state agency to
local administration effective July 1, 2023 (FY 2024).

Programs
Management Services
Provides internal operations support for all Health Department programs per the rules,
regulations, and policies of federal, state, and County governments; addresses administrative
expectations, activities, and initiatives of the Virginia Department of Health (VDH) in
accordance with its performance contract with the County, and all rules and regulations
promulgated by the Virginia Board of Health, while remaining accountable to the Board of
Supervisors (Board). Management Services activities include strategic planning, human
resources, finance, operations support, quality assurance, and Health Insurance Portability
and Accountability Act (HIPAA) and Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) compliance.

Population Health
Supports Loudoun County’s communitywide roadmap focused on addressing social
determinants of health. This program seeks to improve health and wellness outcomes by
addressing the social determinants of health that challenge the diverse Loudoun community
and by leading the County’s Community Health Assessment (CHA) process.

Epidemiology and Emergency Preparedness
Provides disease surveillance and prevention and public health emergency preparedness
and response activities including, but not limited to, pandemic preparedness. This program
aims to limit the spread of communicable diseases in the community and enhance public
health safeguards through collaboration, strategic planning, workforce development, and
Loudoun Medical Reserve Corps (MRC) unit growth.

_________________________________________________________________________________________________________

_________________________________________________________________________________________________________

Clinical Health Services
Provides communicable disease control, patient care, nursing home screenings, and nutrition
services to Loudoun County’s most vulnerable residents, including Women, Infants, and
Children (WIC) nutrition, clinical, and dental services.

Environmental Health
Provides rabies surveillance and education; vital records; restaurant, hotel, and pool
inspections; public health nuisance complaint investigations; and well and septic system
evaluations.

Housing and Community
Development
The Department of Housing and Community Development (DHCD) offers a wide array of
housing options based on whether a household is looking to rent a unit, purchase a first
home, assistance with down payment and/or closing costs, or wants to rehabilitate an existing
home in the County. DHCD also offers gap financing to our partners for the construction,
preservation or renovation of attainable housing in the County.

Programs
Rental and Home Ownership
Executes the County’s affordable homeownership and rental programs including the
purchase and rental Affordable Dwelling Unit (ADU) Programs, the purchase and rental
Unmet Housing Needs Unit (UHNU) Programs, the Down Payment/Closing Cost Assistance
(DPCC) & DPCC Plus Programs, the Public Employee Homeownership Grant (PEG) Program,
the allocation of Virginia Housing’s Sponsoring Partnerships and Revitalizing Communities
(SPARC) Program, and the State Rental Assistance Program (SRAP).

Housing Choice Voucher
Administers the federal Housing Choice Voucher (HCV) Program, which assists very low- and
extremely low-income households in acquiring safe, decent, and affordable housing, by
providing federal rent payment subsidies to private sector landlords to make up the
difference between what the voucher holder can pay (30 percent of monthly income) and the
charged rent (limited to the federally-established fair market rent standard). The program
fosters self-sufficiency and ensures that properties meet Federal National Standards for the
Physical Inspection of Real Estate (NSPIRE).

Entitlement Grants
Administers federally-funded grants including the Community Development Block Grant
(CDBG) Program and the HOME Investment Partnerships Program (HOME) to address
community and economic development needs and services for low- to moderate-income
residents.

Housing Production, Policy and Internal Operations
Manages housing finance and production initiatives; facilitates policy development and
identifies potential programmatic approaches to address unmet housing needs, initiates new
housing programs, and coordinates legislative review and action; supports several advisory
committees appointed by the Board of Supervisors; manages the Housing Fund; ensures
efficient and effective operations by providing DHCD programs with resources, materials,
and data; and provides timely and informational customer service to the public.

• This approved request includes one regular full-time finance
specialist position in the Department of Housing and
Community Development to maintain the current service level of
its internal operations, specifically the financial responsibilities
associated with new and existing housing programs.
• In November 2023, the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban
Development awarded $2.6 million of housing assistance
funding for the Housing Choice Voucher (HCV) program. Funds
were used to assist HCV program participants, including the
addition of 157 new households receiving monthly HCV rental
subsidies.
• Rent payments must be sent to landlords each month and the
increased volume of payments to be processed requires
existing salaried employees to consistently work outside of
normal working hours to meet contractual payment dates. This
workload increase is further impacted by the expansion or
creation of other housing programs that are managed by the
Department and may lead to staff burnout.
• The finance specialist will maintain current service levels
supporting the financial responsibilities of housing programs
managed by the Department. The finance specialist will review
and process accounts payable/receivable, budget
adjustments, reconciliations, and check runs for the HCV & State
Rental Assistance Program (SRAP) through a new cloud-based
housing management software that was implemented by the
Department in Summer 2025.

Human Resources
The Department of Human Resources (DHR) provides centralized support to County agencies
and the County Administrator in human resources management. DHR strategically recruits,
develops, and retains a highly qualified and diverse workforce in service of the County’s
mission in addition to maintaining a professional and safe work environment.

Programs
Staffing and Compensation
Provides countywide recruitment and selection services, manages human resources data for
recordkeeping and analytics, and administers the County’s classification structure and
compensation plans.

Benefits and Risk Management
Administers benefit and wellness programs for employees and retirees, and provides
oversight of programs and processes to mitigate employment-related risk.

Workforce Relations and Development
Administers employee and labor relations functions and provides learning and organizational
development opportunities to address workforce needs.

Systems and Internal Operations
Administers the Human Resources Information System (HRIS); manages office operations
including budget, financial, and procurement support; and provides administrative support
across DHR functional areas.

• These positions will address an increasing workload for the
Staffing and Compensation program area.
• The number of employment applications has doubled since
FY 2023, from approximately 30,000 in FY 2023 to over 60,000
in FY 2025, due to a wider pool of applicants through the
County's new recruitment system, NeoGov; a 12 percent
increase in recruitments due to a growing workforce; and
changing labor market conditions. This has led to challenges in
meeting the targeted 3-day timeline for screening applications
and referring qualified applicants to departments, which
decreased from 86 percent to 77 percent in the last year.
• The workforce planning specialist will assist with meeting
recruitment demands as well as backfilling capacity on the team
that has been dedicated to providing functional system support
for the NeoGov platform to help leverage its full capabilities.
• The classification and compensation analyst will address
rising requests for reclassifications (64 percent increase
between FY 2023 and FY 2025), salary offer reviews, equity
reviews, and reorganizations. Current staff capacity is stretched,
leading to longer turnaround times for tasks needed to fill
vacant positions, and challenges addressing proactive needs
such as internal salary equity reviews and benchmarking
positions to maintain the County's pay structure.
• In April 2025, the Board doubled the number of official market
comparators from four regional jurisdictions to eight,
increasing the time needed to complete benchmarking for
salary surveys and classification reviews.

Information Technology
The Department of Information Technology (DIT) provides enterprise data center
infrastructure services, technologies in support of County department business operations,
enterprise data solutions, broadband support, communication systems, and technology
services to the County government and Loudoun County Public Schools (LCPS). DIT also
provides radio services and Emergency Communications Center (ECC) technology support
to the County’s public safety agencies and emergency medical staff. Assistance and services
are also provided to the County’s incorporated Towns and County staff that use stateprovided equipment and networks. The Department provides services 24 hours per day,
seven days per week.

Programs
Infrastructure and Customer Service
Provides support, troubleshooting, and assistance to County staff, including management of
end-user devices, networks, servers, and training, as well as broadband and cable TV
franchise oversight. Conducts asset management and manages telephone and duplicating
services for the County.

Enterprise Systems Support
Provides support, troubleshooting, consultation, and analysis for enterprise applications and
data.

Public Safety Support
Provides support for Computer-Aided Dispatch, 911 systems, the radio system, and the
Emergency Communications Center (ECC).

Technology Services
Supports DIT with administrative and management services, professional standards, financial
and budget management, procurement, payroll, and human resources management. Leads
collaboration between financial and IT operations planning.

Security
Manages security posture for the County. Conducts risk analysis, vulnerability assessments,
and cybersecurity awareness training. Provides recommendations on technologies,
infrastructure, and data protection for all County systems.

Project Management Office
Provides DIT with project portfolio analysis and strategic direction as well as training on
processes and tools, including meeting with departments to understand their technology-

Revenue/Local Tax Funding
DIT is primarily funded by local tax
funding (99 percent). Programmatic
revenue primarily consists of
communications tax revenue, which the
Commonwealth distributes to each
locality based on a set percentage
which the County splits between DIT,
Fire and Rescue, and the Sheriff’s
Office. This revenue has remained flat
or declined in recent years as
consumers continue transitioning away
from taxable services including landline
telephones, cable television, and

Expenditure
Operating and maintenance (O&M) costs make up 74 percent of DIT’s expenditures. Large
contracts for productivity and collaboration platforms, enterprise resource planning systems,
and public safety dispatch and communication platforms make up a significant portion of the
Department’s operating expenditures. As the County has grown and added new staff and
facilities, and as staff increasingly relies on technology products, technology costs including
license fees, maintenance, and support have correspondingly increased each year. O&M
costs have also increased to maintain the security and resiliency of the County’s network and
systems as the IT environment continues to evolve. Personnel costs comprise the balance of
DIT’s expenditure budget (26 percent) and have primarily increased due to compensation,
including merit increases approved for the general workforce in each fiscal year.1

Overview

• The Department of Information Technology (DIT) received one
security operations manager position to address span-ofcontrol challenges within DIT’s Security Program.
• This position enhances the Activity's current service level of
detecting and mitigating cyber-attacks by improving oversight
of security operations, incident response, and risk
management activities, ensuring alignment with industry
standards.
• DIT will shift supervisory responsibility for five personnel to
the operations manager, allowing them to focus on operational
execution and day-to-day team management.
• The operations manager will also oversee incident validation
and response coordination between internal teams and
external partners, ensuring that automated outputs translate into
actionable remediation without delays or miscommunication.
• The Chief Information Security Officer will oversee the
operations manager and remain the primary point of contact for
all major initiatives, including capital projects, strategic
planning, compliance oversight, software security reviews, and
countywide cybersecurity governance.

Library Services
Library Services’ mission is to inspire, inform, innovate, and welcome all. Library Services
advances this mission by building community through resources, programs, and services that
celebrate the joy of reading and learning.

Programs
Public Services
Provides patrons access to Loudoun County Public Library’s online and physical collections,
programs, technology, space, and services (including passport, notary, and specialized
services). Promotes the joy of reading and lifelong learning through readers' advisory, early
literacy, teen initiatives, and programs in humanities, arts, and technology, along with
community engagement and educational opportunities. Serves as the community’s
information hub. Partners with community organizations to raise awareness of services
offered.

Support Services
Selects, acquires, catalogs, and processes library materials to inform, educate, and enlighten
patrons. Also provides systems administration, technical training, and support for all
automated library systems and related technologies.

General Library Administration
Enacts the policies of the Library Board of Trustees and Loudoun County government.
Provides administrative support and oversees the Public Services and Support Services
programs. Manages the budget, accounting, human resources, training needs, and Capital
Improvement Program (CIP) for Library Services.

Mapping and Geographic
Information
The Office of Mapping and Geographic Information (MAGI or OMAGI) provides centralized
Geographic Information System (GIS) services to County departments, the public, and the
private sector. A significant portion of the work performed by MAGI staff involves creating,
maintaining, managing, analyzing, and distributing spatial data. MAGI staff creates and
maintains maps as well as develops web applications for use by the Board of Supervisors,
County staff, the public, and the private sector. MAGI staff manages the GIS software and
infrastructure in collaboration with the Department of Information Technology (DIT) that
supports the GIS. The land records data created and maintained by the Land Records
Program is integrated with other County systems. MAGI staff collaborates with staff
performing GIS work in other departments. GIS’ qualitative benefits include improved
collaboration, better decision-making, and more efficient business processes. MAGI staff
manages the yearly contract to collect aerial photography and map the planimetric and
topographic features that are a core part of the County’s GIS data. Through the use of GIS,
County staff maps land development activity; maps and maintains conservation easements
data; maintains street centerline data; maps and provides analytical support for County
initiatives; assigns addresses, street names, and parcel identification numbers (PINs); and
performs many other services. GIS data feeds a number of County systems or processes, such
as Public Safety Computer-Aided Dispatch (CAD), and permits. GIS data is also a significant
component of LandMARC, the County’s online land management system. County staff have
access to the Office’s web-mapping system, including intranet-mapping tools or data for the
County’s building inspectors, assessors, and public safety agencies.

Programs
Public Information
Provides assistance and distributes GIS data and information to the public, the private sector,
and other County agencies.

System Development and Support Services (DSS)
Provides the critical administration, services, and application development that support the
functions of the GIS as well as GIS integration with County systems.

Development and Analysis
Develops maps, analyzes, and maintains geospatial data; i.e., mappable data layers used by
the GIS or shared through the GeoHub, which is a central website featuring interactive map
applications, informative dashboards, and story maps.

Land Records Maintenance
Maintains parcels, addresses, and street information, per Loudoun County Codified
Ordinances, and then transfers these and other data to various data systems, including public
mapping products, the County’s CAD system, and the United States Postal Services.

Mental Health, Substance Abuse, and
Developmental Services
The mission of the Department of Mental Health, Substance Abuse, and Developmental
Services (MHSADS) is to promote mental, behavioral, and developmental health and wellness
by connecting individuals and their families with person-centered, recovery-oriented services
and supports in partnership with the Loudoun community.

Programs
Residential Services
Provides community residential living service options in a variety of settings.

Community-Based Support Services
Provides therapies and case management to support infants and toddlers with
developmental delays. Provides treatments and supports for adults living with a
developmental disability or serious mental illness to work, volunteer, and engage in activities
throughout the community.

Crisis Services
Provides immediate, intensive and time-limited crisis intervention and resolution services.
Activities include community-based crisis response, emergency evaluation and assessment
for people experiencing a psychiatric crisis.

Outpatient Services
Provides behavioral health treatment to individuals and families through therapy,
psychoeducation, psychological evaluation, psychiatric evaluation, medication, and medical
management. Some services are clinic based and others are provided in the community.

Outreach and Coordination Services
Promotes behavioral health awareness to strengthen resilience and foster wellness. Activities
increase public awareness, link individuals to support by assessing strengths and needs,
coordinate care across providers, facilitate linkage to resources, and intervene in behavioral
health crises.

Business Operations
Provides internal operations support for all MHSADS programs in accordance with the rules,
regulations, and policies of Federal, State, and County Government; addresses administrative
expectations of the Virginia Department of Behavioral Health and Developmental Services
(DBHDS) Performance Contract while remaining accountable to the direction of the Board of
Supervisors (Board) and coordinating with the Community Services Board (CSB).

Mental Health Substance Abuse and Developmental Services Priority 1: Contract Funding for
Supervised Living Homes
Personnel:

Details

Overview

Service Current Service Level
Level: Request
Mandates: Not mandated
Program: Residential Services
Activity: Supervised Living
One-time $0
LTF:
Recurring $650,000
LTF:

• This approved request provides funding to contract the
operation of three existing supervised living facilities from
County staff to a qualified vendor. A contracted vendor at these
supervised living facilities is part of a strategic shift for the
Department of Mental Health, Substance Abuse, and
Developmental Services (MHSADS), which aims to move existing
staff from supervised living to County group homes to meet
current service levels of the Residential Services program.
• MHSADS is the only provider of group home services for
individuals living with serious mental illness in Loudoun County.
The realignment of staff from supervised living to group homes
will reduce MHSADS’ reliance on overtime and align its group
homes activity with appropriate staffing levels. Implementation
of this request is expected to positively impact staff morale,
reduce overtime utilization, and provide more continuous high
quality service to residents, thereby positively impacting health
and safety.
• The Board’s 2024-2027 Strategic Initiative 6.2 provides
community programs and services assess the County’s
outsourcing of services, identify which services should be
inhouse, and clarify the relative costs. Contracting this service
provides a cost-effective approach to maintain high-quality care
for existing supervised living residents and allows MHSADS to
address workforce needs in County group homes.

Parks, Recreation, and Community
Services (PRCS)
The mission of Parks, Recreation, and Community Services (PRCS) is to connect all
communities through exceptional people, parks, and programs. This is done in Loudoun
County through the provision of recreational, educational, wellness, culture, and supportive
programming opportunities to County residents.

Programs
Maintenance, Parks, Sports, and Events
Provides high-quality outdoor park facilities; open space; nature, outdoor, and cultural
programs and services; and management of park facilities. Maintains and repairs PRCS
property, facilities, vehicles, and equipment; provides services in emergency response
situations. Provides youth and adults with opportunities to participate in athletics in both
competitive and recreational environments to learn and develop lifelong skills. Provides
quality, large-scale special events that allow residents and visitors to socialize and create
community.

Centers and Aquatics
Provides direct programs, services, and facility management. Manages the following regional
and neighborhood facilities: seven community centers, five senior centers, three recreation
centers, two outdoor pools, and one stand-alone aquatic center. Delivers programs and
services to include, but not limited to, preschool, childcare, camps, trips, fitness, aquatic,
enrichment, specialty programs, special events, rentals, senior adult programs which
encompass home-delivered and congregate meals and volunteer opportunities.

Community Services
Provides middle school and high school-aged youth with opportunities in recreational,
educational, and cultural events that promote leadership development and positive choices.
Provides after-school programs for elementary and middle school-aged children, adaptive
recreation, and summer and specialty camps that build leisure, social, and physical skills
through diverse and developmentally appropriate recreational and educational programs.
Aging Services plans, implements, and promotes services and programs including
recreational, educational, and physical fitness classes; and social activities to enhance wellbeing, independence, and quality of life for older adults and their caregivers. Provides
accessible leisure and recreational opportunities for County residents with cognitive and
physical disabilities.

Departmental Support and Operations
Provides human resources management, facility management, planning and development,
training, public relations, communications, marketing, programming and customer service

Planning and Zoning
The mission of the Department of Planning and Zoning (DPZ) is to assist decision-makers in
shaping and managing the County’s land use goals through ongoing community outreach,
comprehensive policy and regulatory recommendations, and timely development review.

Programs
Land Use Review
Leads the evaluation and processing of legislative land development applications through
project management, technical recommendations, and public presentations.

Community Planning
Oversees the policy development process, including community outreach; and administers
and interprets the Comprehensive Plan, including growth management and historic
preservation.

Administration
Provides leadership and overall direction; implements County policies and procedures.

Zoning Administration
Administers and interprets zoning ordinances, proffers, and special exception conditions

Zoning Enforcement
Ensures that the local zoning ordinances, the Virginia Maintenance Code, and designated
sections of Loudoun County Codified Ordinances are effectively, consistently, and fairly
enforced.

Customer Service Center
Delivers "first-tier" internal and external customer service for staff, residents, elected officials,
and applicants navigating the development process.

Special Projects
Oversees and manages Board-prioritized planning initiatives, including Comprehensive Plan
amendments, Zoning Ordinance amendments and planning-related special studies, in
coordination with other DPZ programs and internal and external stakeholders.

• The FY 2027 Adopted Budget for the Department of Planning
and Zoning includes one supervising zoning inspector, four
additional zoning inspectors and one planning technician to
provide the Zoning Enforcement Division with sufficient staff to
enhance their level of service. Should the Board vote to adopt
additional provisions of the Virginia Property Maintenance
Code (VPMC), these additional resources will enable the
Zoning Enforcement Division to effectively implement and
enforce these regulations. These positions will also ensure
more than 95 percent of complaints are responded to within 48
business hours.
• Should the Board adopt additional provisions of the VPMC,
there will be an increased need for supervisory interaction and
intervention. Thus, the supervising zoning inspector is
necessary to provide adequate and effective daily supervision
and mentoring of new and existing staff.
• The four zoning inspectors will enable managers to train new
hires and delegate caseloads equitably in anticipation of the
Board adopting additional provisions of the VPMC.
Furthermore, these resources will relieve the excessive
caseloads that zoning inspectors are currently managing.
•The planning technician will provide the Zoning Enforcement
Division with a full-time position dedicated to administrative
support. This position will be responsible for complaint intake,
and case monitoring in LEx and LandMARC, enabling
supervisors and zoning inspectors to focus on case
remediation and working with constituents to resolve
complaints.

Sheriff’s Office
The Loudoun County Sheriff’s Office (LCSO) works to continuously improve safety and law
enforcement services to all members of the community through the STEP-Up Strategy of
improved service, technology, efficiency, and professionalism. LCSO works interactively with
federal, state, and other local law enforcement authorities to enforce criminal laws by sharing
capabilities, strategies, and assets. LCSO partners with community service groups and human
services agencies to implement strategies that improve the quality of life for Loudoun County
residents, businesses, and visitors.

Programs
Criminal Investigations
The Criminal Investigations Division (CID) actively investigates criminal offenses and conducts
thorough follow-up inquiries into cases referred by other divisions within LCSO, as well as
from various County departments and federal, state, and local law enforcement agencies.
The division is responsible for investigating major crimes, including homicides, robberies,
serious crimes against individuals, special victim cases, and financial/cybercrime offenses.
CID oversees all forensic service requirements for the department through its Crime Scene
Unit, Biometric Examination Unit, and Digital Forensic Unit. Additionally, CID manages
investigations related to drugs and gangs as well as providing intel support for the agency.

Field Operations
Keeps the citizens and visitors of Loudoun safe by providing professional incident response,
proactive crime reduction strategies, and genuine community outreach. All Field Operations
patrol or station deputies are assigned to one of four geographic station areas. Deputies are
the initial response to all calls for service and patrol the County 24 hours per day, 365 days of
the year. Patrol staff and leadership engage the community through outreach and
communications strategies that improve the quality of life for County residents, businesses,
and visitors.

Operational Support
Provides specialized operational support services to the Loudoun County Sheriff’s Office
through traffic safety and enforcement initiatives, emergency management coordination,
specialty response teams, crime prevention programming, youth education, wellness
initiatives, and school safety operations. The Operational Support Division oversees the
School Resource Officer Unit, Crossing Guard Unit, Crime Prevention and Community
Outreach functions, Specialty Dockets and Co-Responder initiatives, and multiple countywide
support programs. The Division also oversees employee wellness and resiliency programs
focused on enhancing workforce readiness, supporting employee well-being, and
strengthening organizational effectiveness.
The Division also manages the Special Operations Section, which includes the Tactical
Support Unit, K-9 Unit, Civil Disturbance Unit, Search and Rescue/Personal Locator
_________________________________________________________________________________________________________

Loudoun.gov/Budget

Loudoun.gov/ProgramReview

_________________________________________________________________________________________________________

Services/sUAS teams, Honor Guard, Crisis Negotiation Team, Explosive Ordnance Disposal
Team, and other specialized collateral response teams that support agency operations and
critical incidents. Emergency Management staff assigned to the Division coordinate with
Loudoun County agencies, regional partners, and Sheriff’s Office leadership on emergency
preparedness, contingency planning, and large-scale event coordination.

Corrections
Operates the Loudoun County Adult Detention Center and Community Custody Program by
providing a safe, secure, and healthy environment to house both pretrial and sentenced
inmates. Works closely with other County agencies and local partners to reduce recidivism by
providing inmates with job and life skills, educational programming, mental health services
and counseling, and addiction treatment.

Court Services
Provides security for the Loudoun County Courts Complex and enforces civil processes in
Loudoun County. Additionally, it ensures detainee presence in courts and provides security
for off-site hearings as ordered.

Administrative and Technical Services (ATS)
Provides critical support functions to LCSO divisions, including records management,
property and evidence management, accreditation and training, human resources, IT
support, false alarm reduction, employment services, and finance and administration.
Responsibilities include delivering comprehensive training programs for both law
enforcement personnel and civilian staff to ensure adherence to best practices and
established protocols. Additionally, this area provides emergency 9-1-1 dispatch and nonemergency telecommunicator services, while also managing administrative calls for service.

Office of the Sheriff
Provides senior command and leadership, strategic planning, internal review, and Public
Information Office functions.

• The Adopted Budget provides the first of two planned phases
of staffing related to the Adult Detention Center (ADC)
Expansion/Phase 3 capital project. This phase provides 26
uniformed staff positions for the housing area component of the
related project.
• The identified phasing approach will facilitate
recruitment/background check and academy training timelines
ahead of the facility's expansion opening for operations.
• Twenty of the positions are deputies and will staff the
applicable shifts needed for the planned housing area. Four
positions are sergeants and will supervise and manage the
individual shift teams. Two positions, a first lieutenant and a
second lieutenant, will provide overall leadership and
supervision of this new housing area in the expanded ADC
ecosystem while supporting division leadership, generally.
• The staffing of this initial phase is consistent with staffing
plans identified in and through the Community Based
Corrections Plan completed in December 2021 and will allow
for operation of a housing area that accommodates inmate
programming and lower custody level inmates using a hybrid
supervision design.

Transportation and Capital
Infrastructure
The Department of Transportation and Capital Infrastructure (DTCI) leads the planning,
design, utility relocation, and construction of transportation and facility capital projects for the
County through the Capital Improvement Program (CIP); and assists with the preparation of
the capital budget. DTCI is also responsible for long-range transportation planning, and
traffic engineering. DTCI staff serves as technical advisors to the Board of Supervisors (Board)
on matters relating to transportation, facility development, regional funding, project
scheduling, and cost estimating.

Programs
Design and Construction
Collaborates with the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) to develop the CIP budget,
schedules, and scopes. Oversees the financial management of capital project accounts with
multiple funding sources and prepares and monitors DTCI’s operating budget. Manages the
planning, design, utility relocation, and construction of capital transportation and facilities
projects while ensuring compliance with applicable federal, state, and local laws, standards,
and specifications. Provides quality control and delivery of projects on schedule and within
budget.

Transportation Planning and Traffic Engineering
Develops, manages revisions to, and ensures compliance with the Countywide
Transportation Plan, acting as a referral agency in the community development process.
Performs traffic and transportation modeling, safety and operational studies, and special
transportation-related studies and evaluations. Performs traffic and highway engineering
services to address community traffic and parking complaints. Manages the Residential
Permit Parking Program. Coordinates transportation planning and funding with regional
partners and funding organizations. Monitors and develops grant funding applications for
transportation projects and programs. Supports OMB on matters related to capital facility
standards and capital intensity factors.

Administration & Policy
Delivers a broad range of strategic support functions, including human resource
administration and management, Board and public coordination and communication,
budget development and monitoring, department policy development and enhancement,
technology support, asset management, and oversight of the capital program management
office, along with procurement and accounting activities essential to the County’s capital
program.

Budget staff ensure appropriate funding for capital projects and operational needs and
complete required budget adjustments. Communications staff manages Board and public
outreach, coordinates project‑related ceremonies and engagement efforts and ensures
timely and accurate dissemination of project updates to the community. Accounting and
procurement staff oversee accurate and timely vendor purchase order submissions and
invoice processing, validate reimbursements to external agencies, and reconcile daily project
expenditures. Technology staff administer project management and related software systems
and provide Audio/Visual and technical support. Human resources responsibilities include
recruiting and onboarding new employees and managing employee relations. Staff also fulfill
Freedom of Information Act requests, coordinate Board item submissions, and support
communication with Board offices.
Additionally, the division provides essential administrative assistance to support overall
operations.

Treasurer
The Treasurer is a locally elected constitutional officer whose duties are mandated by the
Code of Virginia and local ordinances. The Treasurer is elected at-large for a four-year term
and provides direct service to all Loudoun residents and businesses. The principal functions
of the Treasurer’s Office include billing and collecting taxes for real and personal property,
business licenses, and other services as specified by the Code of Virginia and local
ordinances; acting as primary depository of revenue for all County agencies, including
Loudoun County Public Schools (LCPS); investing and safeguarding County funds;
reconciling County funds to bank and investment accounts; and providing outstanding
customer service to taxpayers, County staff, and LCPS staff.

Program
Administration of the Revenue
Collect real and tangible personal property taxes for the County and all seven incorporated
towns and serve as the depository for cash receipts for all County and LCPS agencies.

Youth Services
The Youth Services Department operates the Loudoun County Juvenile Detention Center
(JDC) and the RISE (Reaching for Insight, Success, and Empowerment) Youth Shelter for
court-involved youth. The department also provides prevention and engagement services for
at-risk youth and their families at the Youth and Family Resource Center to link them to
community-based supports.
A group of staff in the department, formerly known as the Juvenile Court Service Unit,
previously provided direct support to the 20th District Court Service Unit (CSU) under a
contract with the Virginia Department of Juvenile Justice (DJJ). Following a change in DJJ
purview, effective October 2024, CSU functions in Loudoun are now solely administered by
state employees. The County needed to update the department’s name to reflect the
distinction and selected Youth Services. County Administration and internal operations
departments have been working with Youth Services’ leadership to redesign administrative
services and programming and adjust the work activities of employees who previously
provided services to the CSU. Staff supporting residential services did not experience a
change; however, the County has been working with all department staff to review
opportunities for department-wide efficiencies. The department’s system reorganization was
completed by July 1, 2025. The administrative services and program redesign components
continued throughout fiscal year 2026 and remain under development.

Programs
Administrative Services
Provides leadership and overall direction; implements County policies and procedures.

Prevention and Engagement Services
Assists youth and their families to help prevent or reduce involvement with law enforcement
and/or the juvenile justice system. Provides referrals to community-based supports to
Loudoun youth demonstrating risky behavior. Provides diversion services, evidence-based
prevention, educational programming, and community service opportunities.

Residential Services
Provides safe and secure, out-of-home placements for youth with a goal of providing positive
development for youth while in care. Services include a secure detention providing long-term
and short-term secure placement and a secure, short-term shelter program for youth
involved in the court system.

Total – Non-Departmental Expenditures

Compensation Increases. The FY 2027 Adopted Budget includes funding for compensation
increases as follows: a 4.25 percent merit increase for eligible regular employees on the
general workforce pay plan; a salary scale increase of 2.5 percent and a one-step merit
increase for eligible uniformed Fire and Rescue employees; and a salary scale increase of
5.75 percent and a one-step merit increase for eligible uniformed Sheriff’s deputies. The
general workforce merit increase covers the General Government bargaining unit and
corresponds to the ratified collective bargaining agreement with the Service Employees
International Union (SEIU) Virginia 512. For the Fire and Rescue bargaining unit, this funding
covers the uniformed pay increases and other compensation-related provisions included in
the ratified collective bargaining agreement with the International Association of Fire Fighters
(IAFF) Local 3756. Additional provisions include incremental adjustments to specialty pay and
a 5.5 percent merit increase for employees who are on the general workforce pay plan but
included in the Fire and Rescue bargaining unit. For the Sheriff’s Office, funding is also
included for adjustments to various stipends, including the canine handler stipend, field
training officer stipend, and clothing allowance, to maintain regional competitiveness in line
with the Board’s compensation philosophy.
The FY 2027 Adopted Budget also includes a 2 percent adjustment to the range
minimum and maximum of each grade in the general workforce open range pay plan, which
does not impact employee salaries unless they fall below the adjusted range minimum. In
comparison, salary scale adjustments to public safety grade and step pay plans provide an
additional pay increase to employees by increasing the value of each grade and step.
Salary scale adjustments are budgeted to take effect at the beginning of the fiscal year.
The merit and step increases are budgeted to begin with the second pay period in
September 2026 (paid out with the first paycheck in October). The Board’s approved
compensation philosophy is to deliver pay (average salaries) within a range of 100 to 105
percent of the average mid-point of Loudoun’s comparator market, which is defined as the
Counties of Arlington (VA), Fairfax (VA), Prince William (VA), Montgomery (MD), Frederick
(MD), and Prince George’s (MD); the City of Alexandria; and the District of Columbia. A
summary of recent compensation increases is provided in the tables below.

EMPACT Awards. County policies include provisions to permit individual and team bonus
awards in recognition of outstanding achievement. These provisions are important tools for
supporting an organization that recognizes and rewards excellent performance. Funding for
EMPACT awards in the FY 2027 Adopted Budget has been incrementally adjusted based on
the continued growth of the County workforce.
Personnel Vacancy Savings. The County budgets anticipated savings resulting from
employee turnover in the Non-Departmental budget. This amount is evaluated annually and
adjusted to reflect actual savings, which occur through expenditure balances in departments’
personnel budgets. Personnel vacancy savings are budgeted at a rate of 5.3 percent of salary
and related fringe benefits in the FY 2027 Adopted Budget.
Annual and Sick Leave Payouts. Payout of annual and sick leave balances upon employees’
departures from employment is included in the Non-Departmental budget and allocated to
departments’ personnel budgets as needed throughout the year.

Length of Service Award Program (LOSAP). This is a benefit for volunteer firefighters
previously budgeted in Loudoun County Fire and Rescue’s departmental budget. This
budget is included in the Non-Departmental budget to comply with Governmental
Accounting Standards Board (GASB) statement #73.
Other Post-Employment Benefits (OPEB) Contribution. This represents the County’s
contribution to the OPEB Trust Fund for retiree health insurance benefits. More information
on the County OPEB Trust Fund is available in the Other Funds section.
Retiree Health Insurance. Funding was included to cover expenditures for retiree health
insurance plans on a “pay-as-you-go” basis in the FY 2026 Adopted Budget. For FY 2027, the
OPEB Trust is projected to have sufficient funding for the County to resume withdrawing from
the Trust to cover the County’s share of retiree health insurance costs. Therefore, a separate
allocation for “pay-as-you-go” financing of benefits is not included in the FY 2027 Adopted
Budget.
Hiring Incentive Program. In April 2023, the Board approved amendments to Chapter
252.02, Bonuses, of the Loudoun County Code of Ordinances that authorized the County
Administrator to implement a hiring and retention incentive program. A hiring and retention
incentive program was implemented in April 2024, with the purpose of addressing
challenging recruitment conditions for certain hard-to-fill positions and maintaining
competitiveness with comparator jurisdictions. The FY 2027 Adopted Budget contains
continued funding for this program.
Deferred Compensation Match. The FY 2026 Adopted Budget contained funding to
increase the match for employee contributions to the County’s 457(b) deferred
compensation plan to the greater of $20 or 1 percent of salary per pay period, up to an
annual maximum of $1,000. The increased match has been implemented, and funding was
programmed in department personnel budgets for the FY 2027 Adopted Budget.
Interest Expense. The County budgets interest payments on real and personal property tax
refunds in the Non-Departmental budget.
Payment to Leesburg – Economic Development Payment. At its February 6, 2024
meeting3, the Board reviewed the terms of a mediated agreement and approved the terms of
the agreement, which would allow the Town of Leesburg to annex more than 400 acres of
land known as Compass Creek. As part of the agreement, beginning in FY 2026, the County
will pay Leesburg $2 million (escalated by 3 percent each year) annually to promote
economic development in the Joint Land Management Area outside the town’s limits.
Payment to Nonprofits. This category includes funding provided to nonprofit organizations
through the County’s Human Services Program (including the competitive and core services
provider processes).

3 February 4, 2024, Business Meeting, Item 5, Proposed Settlement of Leesburg’s Annexation.

Payment to Regional and Intergovernmental Organizations. The County provides
funding to many regional and intergovernmental organizations from which the County
receives operational support. Regional organizations include the Metropolitan Washington
Council of Governments and the Northern Virginia Regional Park Authority, both serving
multi-jurisdictional areas. Intergovernmental organizations include other localities in Loudoun
County, such as the Town of Leesburg, which receives funds to support School Resource
Officers in Leesburg area schools. Beginning in FY 2027, the non-departmental expenditures
pages reflect only contributions budgeted in the non-departmental budget, including salary
supplements. FY 2026 Adopted amounts reflect the incorporation of salary supplements in
the Payment to Regional and Intergovernmental Organizations line. More information can be
found in the Regional and Intergovernmental Organization section.
Payment to the Economic Development Authority (EDA). Beginning in FY 2021, the
County provides funding to the EDA as part of a 15-year incentive to bring the United States
Customs and Border Protection Agency’s Office of Information Technology (OIT) to Quantum
Park in Ashburn. This economic development incentive was agreed to by the Board at the
March 22, 2018 Business Meeting, and payments started on January 1, 2021.
Payment to Loudoun County Public Schools. The FY 2027 Adopted Budget includes a
payment to Loudoun County Public Schools (LCPS) for the local contribution to the school
division. The payment supports the LCPS Operating, Capital Improvement Program (CIP),
and Capital Asset Preservation Program (CAPP) at the following levels.

requests in the FY 2027 Adopted Budget include two types of expenditures: departmental
and non-departmental. Non-departmental costs include those coordinated by other
departments in support of the requests, including the purchase of technology, furniture,
vehicles, and associated office renovations. These non-departmental one-time costs are

shown here.

Transfer to Children’s Services Act Fund. The Children’s Services Act is funded through a
state pool of monies allocated to each locality, which requires a local match. Annual transfers
are made to this fund to provide for the County’s match.
Transfer to Legal Resource Center Fund. In recent fiscal years, revenues for the Legal
Resource Center Fund (Law Library) have not been sufficient to fund planned expenditures. A
transfer of local tax funding is budgeted to this fund; in the past, a supplemental budget
adjustment of General Fund revenue balanced the revenue shortfall during the fiscal year.
Transfer to Transportation District Fund. The Transportation District Fund was created in
FY 2013 to segregate transportation and transit-related revenues and expenditures. The
County is required to enact a Commercial & Industrial (C&I) Property Tax at $0.125 per $100
valuation or dedicate an equivalent level of funding for transportation and transit purposes to
be eligible to receive the 30 percent share of Northern Virginia Transportation Authority
(NVTA) revenue, as discussed in this document. To date, the Board of Supervisors has taken
no action to levy a C&I Property Tax, and the County dedicates equivalent funding from
general revenues. As state law mandates, this funding is allocated in the Transportation
District Fund, having been transferred from the non-departmental budget of the General
Fund.
Transfer to the Rivana Community Development Authority (CDA) Fund. The Rivana CDA
Fund is established to collect tax increment, special assessment, and special tax collections
on real property for the purpose of paying debts of the authority to finance and construction
public infrastructure at the Rivana at Innovation Station development. Pursuant to the Rivana
Memorandum of Agreement, excess tax revenues above the 2019 assessed values of the
properties within the CDA are to be collected and transferred to the CDA for part of the debt
service needs incurred.
Transfer to Capital Projects Fund. The transfer represents the allocation of local tax funding
sent from the General Fund to the Capital Projects Fund.

Transfer to Capital Asset Preservation Program Fund. The Board established the Capital
Asset Preservation Fund (CAPP) as a consistent means of planning and financing major
maintenance and repair efforts for County facilities. Annual transfers are made to provide
funding for these efforts. Since FY 2023, CAPP also includes the budget for organization-wide
personal computer replacement, formerly part of the General Fund. Additional information is
available in the Other Appropriated Funds section.
Transfer to Major Equipment Replacement Fund. Funding is provided to replace major
equipment valued over $5,000.
Transfer to Debt Service Fund. Local tax funding pays principal and interest on financed
capital improvement projects.
Transfer to Self-Insurance Fund. Risk management and workers’ compensation costs are
funded by annual transfers to the County’s Self-Insurance Fund.
Transfer to Affordable Housing Fund. Local tax funding dedicated to affordable housing
programs is budgeted in the Non-Departmental budget and transferred to the Affordable
Housing Fund. As of FY 2026 Adopted Budget, the amount of recurring local tax funding
support is equivalent to one cent of the real property tax rate, which was increased from the
one-half cent budgeted in previous fiscal years. In the FY 2027 Adopted Budget, this amount
is equivalent to one cent of the real property tax rate ($19.4 million) plus 20 percent of
additional local tax funding available above the 9 percent operating budget growth target
set in budget guidance ($6.6 million).4

Landfill Fee Offsets
July 1, 2026 – June 30, 2028
The County Administrative Support Offset Program (CASOP)1 enables the Board of
Supervisors (Board) to make in-kind contributions to local organizations, governmental
entities, and internal County departments without direct use of local tax funding. The Board
approves landfill fee offsets, recognizing that the Loudoun County Solid Waste Management
Facility, by policy, must recover its disposal operations and Capital Improvement Plan costs
through tipping fees.
Qualifying organizations may request that the Board award them an offset of landfill fees.
The Board awards offsets for two years through the biennial CASOP, provided that
organizations remain in compliance with the criteria for the program and the offset amount is
adopted as part of the annual budget. Applicants must agree to meet all of the following
criteria and adhere to the standards below:
1. The organization must file a written request for an offset by providing all the required
information on the Landfill Fee Offset Award Application Form provided by the
County.
2. The organization must be a governmental entity or nonprofit organization with
Internal Revenue Service 501(c)(3) status.
3. The organization must provide a service for the public good, which must be described
in writing on the Landfill Fee Offset Award Application Form. With regard to 501(c)(3)
organizations, prioritization will be given to organizations that can demonstrate their
services result in savings to the taxpayer and provide a direct benefit to the
community.
4. The organization must agree to ensure that its employees/members do not use the
fee offset for disposal of non-organization generated waste.
5. The organization shall not exceed the offset amount granted by the Board of
Supervisors.
6. The organization must agree to only deliver waste that is generated from within
Loudoun County. Waste must be:
a. Municipal Solid Waste (MSW), Construction Demolition Debris (CDD), or
vegetative waste, in accordance with the Virginia Solid Waste Management
Regulations, the County’s Solid Waste facility Permit(s), facility operational
requirements and the Loudoun County Solid Waste Management Plan
requirements.
b. Non-hazardous.
7. The organization must agree to separate waste as directed by County staff.
8. The organization must agree to follow the posted onsite facility rules and directions
from County staff.

1 Previous budget documents referred to the County Administrative Support Offset Program as the

Landfill Fee Waiver Program.
_________________________________________________________________________________________________________

Loudoun.gov/Budget

366

Loudoun.gov/ProgramReview

FY
2027 Adopted Budget
_________________________________________________________________________________________________________

9. The organization must agree to follow all required pre-authorization protocols for
waste requiring special handling.
10. The organization must have a current, active Loudoun County Solid Waste
Management Facility credit account.
The total annual landfill fee offset for the FY 2027 Adopted Budget is $1,134,400 which is
consistent with the total amount available identified in the most recent Financial Analysis of
the Landfill Disposal Operations at the Loudoun County Solid Waste Management Facility
(Financial Analysis). The Financial Analysis is completed annually as part of the budget
development process to project the necessary revenue required to meet operational
obligations.
Organizations receiving fee offsets include Loudoun County Government departments,
Towns within the County, fire and rescue volunteer companies, other government entities,
and nonprofit organizations. Approximately 58 percent of the FY 2027 Adopted Budget
offsets are for Loudoun County Government departments and agencies (including Loudoun
County Public Schools), 12 percent for Town governments, less than 1 percent for volunteer
fire and rescue companies, 26 percent for other government entities, and 4 percent for
nonprofit organizations.1
The upcoming fee offset period is from July 1, 2026, through June 30, 2028. The annual
landfill fee offset for FY 2028 is projected to be consistent with the FY 2027 Adopted Budget.

Nonprofit Organizations1
Based on available resources, the County provides funding allocations to community-based
organizations that deliver services with a direct benefit to vulnerable Loudoun County
residents. The FY 2027 Adopted Budget includes an overall allocation of $8,170,573 for
nonprofit organizations through two distinct programs: the Competitive Grant Program2 and
the Core Service Contracts3.
The Board of Supervisors (Board) continues to improve and refine these two programs based
on recommendations from key stakeholders and County staff. These improvements represent
an effort to strengthen the County’s coordination and collaboration with community partners
and to ensure local funds are leveraged in the most effective manner for the County’s most
vulnerable residents.

Competitive Grant Program
The Competitive Grant Program is designed to leverage local funding in the most effective
manner to assist the County’s most vulnerable and disadvantaged residents in meeting
critical health, safety, security, and independence needs. The FY 2027 Adopted Budget
includes $3,958,331 for the program, which is based on the availability of funding resources
and subject to a competitive process. The FY 2026 Adopted Budget included $2,947,966 for
the competitive grant program; however, on May 20, 2025, the Board approved an
additional $895,073 in FY 2025 fund balance to fully fund the recommended nonprofit
organizations, bringing the total allocation to $3,843,039 for FY 2026.4 This additional

funding was reflected in the revised budget in FY 2026 and annualized for FY 2027. The FY

amount and a 34 percent increase from the FY 2026 adopted budget amount.
For the competitive grant process, a committee of contracted subject matter experts and
the Department of Finance and Procurement review grant applications and develop funding
recommendations for consideration by the Board. On October 13, 2020, the
Finance/Government Operations and Economic Development Committee (FGOEDC)
provided guidance to fund applicants scoring 75 percent or higher in the application review
process.1 Additionally, the FGOEDC provided guidance that a funding gap analysis be
completed each year as part of the process to support budget planning.
The Board also adopted broad Areas of Need categories that focus on the impact or
outcomes that nonprofit programs will have on the community:
•

Prevention and Self-Sufficiency: Services focused on assisting individuals and
families in becoming and/or remaining independent and stable, and providing tools,
skills, strategies, and resources to individuals and families.

•

Crisis Intervention and Diversion: Services provided to individuals and families in
crisis to overcome immediate problems and reduce or prevent further penetration to
more restrictive and expensive higher-level services.

•

Long-Term Support: Services that focus on assisting individuals who have continuing,
long-term support needs to remain healthy, safe, and independent in the community.

•

Improved Quality of Human Services: Services and opportunities provided to
individuals, organizations, and communities that enhance the quality, accessibility,
accountability, and coordination of services provided by community organizations.

In addition to the larger competitive grant process, the Board created a simplified grant
process for mini-grants in amounts up to $5,000. This program involves a simplified
application process for any organization applying for a small grant for the purposes of
capacity building or small-scale innovative ideas or projects. The budget for this mini-grant
program is approximately 3 percent of the total competitive grant process annually and is
deducted from the total competitive grant budget.

Core Service Contracts
Core service providers meet the critical needs of those most vulnerable and disadvantaged in
the community through contracts with the County. With guidance from County
Administration and feedback from the departments of Family Services; Health; Mental Health,
Substance Abuse and Development Services; and Parks, Recreation, and Community
Services, the Department of Finance and Procurement issued requests for proposals for
healthcare services, domestic violence services, independent living services, dental services,
and representative payee services. In FY 2027, the County is anticipated to hold six contracts
for these services that are managed by various departments. The FY 2027 Adopted Budget

Regional and Intergovernmental
Organizations Contributions
Contractual and formulary contributions are made to regional organizations that provide
services on a multi-jurisdictional level on behalf of several localities in the region. Funding is
defined by contractual agreements, and funding requests submitted by each organization
are generally based on a formulary approach. Requests are reviewed by the Office of
Management and Budget. Regional organizations contribute to the economic development,
education, recreation, culture, health, and well-being of the community. Examples include
the Metropolitan Washington Council of Governments (COG), a multi-governmental
organization that supports many of the County’s planning efforts, and the Northern Virginia
Regional Park Authority, a collective effort of Northern Virginia governments to provide
recreational and park opportunities for member jurisdictions. Intergovernmental
contributions are allocated to public entities that provide specific services within their
jurisdiction. The contribution to the Town of Leesburg for school resource officers (SROs) is
considered an intergovernmental contribution. This contribution provides partial funding for
the cost of Leesburg Police SROs located at public middle and high schools located within
the Town of Leesburg.
The FY 2027 Adopted Budget includes an overall allocation of $14,059,413 and local tax
funding in the amount of $12,851,538 for regional and intergovernmental organizations,
which represents an increase of 13 percent compared to the local tax funding for these
contributions in the FY 2026 Adopted Budget. This increase is mostly due to new local tax
funding contributions for regional public safety programs through COG and the Northern
Virginia Emergency Response System that were previously funded through the Urban Area
Security Initiative (UASI) grant from the federal government.
The overall allocation includes $2,397,463 for salary supplements for state employees,
specifically for the Virginia Indigent Defense Commission’s Loudoun Public Defenders Office,
the District Courts, the Virginia Department of Juvenile Justice 20th District Court Services
Unit, the Virginia Department of Corrections District 25 Probation and Parole Office, and the
Virginia Cooperative Extension. It is important to note that in previous budget documents,
except for the contribution to the Public Defenders Office, these salary supplements were not
included in the tables below but instead were included in the Non-Departmental
Expenditures section. For the Loudoun Public Defenders Office, the FY 2026 Adopted
Budget provided a 40 percent salary supplement for eligible state employees and $400,000
for four positions (Mitigation Specialist, Interpreter, Juvenile Case Manager, and Discovery
Specialist); the FY 2027 Adopted Budget provides an additional $211,013 for a new senior
attorney position.
Lastly, the FY 2026 Adopted Budget amounts below are different from those in the FY
2026 Adopted Budget document for several organizations. Contributions to these
organizations were shown exclusively in department budget pages or in the Nonprofit
Organizations section in FY 2026. Those contributions are now represented here to show all
contributions in one place. These organizations are the Loudoun Small Business
Development Center, Northern Virginia Economic Development Alliance, Washington

Revolving Loan Fund
On July 21, 1992, the Board of Supervisors (Board) created the Revolving Loan Fund (RLF), a
portion of the County’s non-spendable General Fund balance. The RLF provided a financing
mechanism for capital projects and the equipment needs of general government, the
schools, and volunteer fire and rescue companies. During the CIP deliberation process on
March 21, 1996, the Board redefined the scope of the RLF by limiting entities that may
receive these funds to future non-general government and non-school requests related to
wastewater treatment projects or volunteer/fire and rescue projects. Further, on September
15, 2020, the Board broadened the RLF to “assist other governmental agencies and volunteer
fire and rescue companies within the geographic boundaries of the County.”1
