Assessed Value and Tax Rates
Assessed Valuation of Residential Property
The fair market value of single-family homes and condominiums in Loudoun (reported as of
each January 1st) increased every year from 1993 through 2006, before declining for four
consecutive years as construction activity declined and market prices dropped in the 2008-09
recession. Growth of residential assessed property value resumed in 2011 and has continued
since. Values between 2011 and 2022 were buoyed by low interest rates and a lack of
available inventory as homeowners delayed listing their homes or sought refinancing
opportunities. Developing in 2022 and continuing into 2025, higher interest rates and
constrained inventory have had a moderating impact on residential property activity.
Residential property values appreciated 1.36 percent during 2025. Residential new
construction and growth activity increased by 1.1 percent during 2025. Development activity
added $1.184 billion to the County’s residential portfolio in 2025.
Multi-family properties, which are valued separately from residential property classes,
appreciated at a faster rate, 5.01 percent. The charts below illustrate the assessed values for
Tax Years (TY) 2016-2026 as well as the forecasted values (*) for TY 2027.

Assessed Valuation of Other Real Property1
The fair market value (FMV) of commercial and industrial property in Loudoun (reported as of
each January 1), grew steadily between 2011 and 2020. On the heels of significant growth in
the data center industry during 2019, the pandemic had a negative impact on assessed
values during 2020. Rates of change varied by property type with the retail and hospitality
sectors experiencing the most significant declines. While commercial properties overall have
recovered, hospitality properties continue to see aggregate assessed values below prepandemic (2019) levels. Total FMV increased significantly in tax year 2026 (over the course of
2025 leading up to January 1, 2026) as data center development continues to surge and as
the local industry continues to perform in a robust fashion and is expected to grow at a
reasonable rate in tax year 2027.

Commercial

FMV for agricultural property fluctuates as properties are rezoned for other uses. The 2026
FMV for agricultural property reflects a revaluation increase of 6.54 percent from tax year
2025. Real property zoned for agricultural use or zoned for commercial use but utilized for
agricultural purposes, may qualify for the County’s Land Use Assessment Program2. Under
this program the property tax due on the difference between the FMV of the land in its
highest and best use and its value in agriculture, horticulture, or open space is deferred until
such time as the property use is subdivided; re-zoned to a more intense, non-agricultural use;
or no longer used for a qualifying purpose. As of January 1, 2026, the value of properties
enrolled in the Land Use Assessment Program totaled approximately $1.61 billion. The charts
below display agricultural values as the taxable values, including the total value of properties
enrolled in the County’s land use assessment program, although it is possible some of these
properties are currently zoned as commercial.

Assessed Value Per Capita
Since 2010, the assessed FMV of real property per capita has steadily increased at varying
rates as real estate prices and construction activity have improved after the 2008-2009
Recession. While 2013 saw significant growth because of appreciation, annual property
appreciation during 2014, 2015, and 2016 was more modest, and most of the increase in the
assessed value per capita during these years was due to the development of new buildings
and parcel improvements. The rate of growth accelerated again in 2017 through 2019, in
large part due to significant commercial investment in the data center industry. Due to the
negative impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic on the values of commercial properties, the
estimated assessed value per capita grew at a slower rate during 2020, resulting in an
estimated assessed value per capita of $233,890 as of January 1, 2021. The increase shown
for January 1, 2026 values reflects continued strong growth in the data center industry
combined with a somewhat more anemic growth rate in the residential portfolio. Forecasted
values for January 1, 2027, reflect continued, but moderate growth in assessed value
expected relative to moderating real property markets.

Residential and Business Property – Share of Real
Property Valuation
As the economy continued to recover from the 2008-2009 Recession, residential properties
comprised around 72 percent of the County’s real property portfolio, while commercial &
industrial properties represented roughly 18 percent. Agricultural, multi-family, and public
service corporation properties made up the remaining 10 percent. Beginning in 2022,
commercial properties have accelerated as a share of real property values, primarily the
result of new construction related to data centers, which tend to have higher assessed values
than other commercial property types. Strong performance in the residential market resulted
in the sector’s accounting for more than 70 percent of the total assessed value up to and
including 2023. Substantial new construction of data centers led to the commercial sector’s
taking on a full 25 percent of the total 2024 assessed value, pushing residential property
down to 67 percent of the total value for the first time since 2009. Residential properties
continue to appreciate, despite recent increases in mortgage rates, because of limited
inventory. Commercial properties grew in 2024 and again substantially in 2025 as the
expected reductive impact of HB 791 failed to materialize. The portfolio saw continued
growth leading into tax year 2026 with this component reaching a full 35 percent of the
portfolio and pushing residential down to 57 percent by comparison. Continued growth is
forecasted for TY 2027.

Property Tax Levy and Percentage of Tax Levy
Collected1
The value of the property tax levy, which includes both real and tangible personal property,
has increased as the County has grown. This growth, along with the percentage of the tax
levy collected within the fiscal year in which the levy occurred, is shown in the following chart.
Collection rates from FY 2011 through FY 2015 were between 98 and 99 percent, leaving $815 million uncollected in the year of the levy. Since then, collection rates have declined to
between 97 and 98 percent, or $35-45 million uncollected. Despite this shift, the County
continues to collect 99 percent of the tax levy over time. This means that any increase in
delinquencies in one year are likely collected in the subsequent year. The COVID-19
pandemic did not have a noticeable impact on collection rates overall, but did produce an
uptick in the value uncollected in the initial year of the levy.

Total Property Tax Levy and Rate of Collection of Tax Levy2

not pursue actions on delinquencies until 90 days after the due date. For TY 2020, the deadline for
personal property taxes was moved from May 5 to June 5 for the convenience of taxpayers due to the

Real Property Assessed Values
Real property assessed values continue to increase as the economy thrives and as Loudoun
grows. While overall growth during 2020 was less than prior years (6.1 percent compared to
a 4-year preceding average of 6.6 percent), it still represented overall growth in the portfolio.
As noted earlier, agricultural values tend to fluctuate as properties are rezoned for other uses.
As shown below, excluding agricultural properties, all classes of property had experienced
growth up until the COVID-19 pandemic. Agricultural values tend to fluctuate as properties
are rezoned for other uses. During 2020 (reflected in TY 2021 values), residential properties
and multi-family properties experienced positive revaluation while commercial properties
experienced negative revaluation. In 2024, the overall portfolio value was originally expected
to decline by about 2.4 percent due to a forecasted drop in the assessed value of commercial
and industrial properties resulting from HB 791. However, this decline did not materialize,
and the overall portfolio value increased by 11.4 percent in 2024 and 18.6 percent in 2025.
2026 saw more modest growth (11.6 percent) as headwinds against the local, state, and
national economies continued to develop. Expectations for modest growth continue into tax
year 2027.

Real Estate, Personal Property, Machinery and
Tools, and Heavy Construction Machinery Tax
Rates
While historically, tax rates for personal property, machinery and tools, and heavy
construction machinery have remained stable for several years, the Tax Year 2023 personal
property tax rate reflects a five-cent reduction to $4.15. The real estate tax rate has changed
more frequently as evidenced in the table below. The tax rates below are per $100 of
assessed value and are set on a calendar year basis. The real estate tax rate is the general,
countywide tax rate and does not include any special district real property levies such as
that for the Metrorail Services District which are assessed on top of the countywide rate. The
FY 2027 Adopted Budget reflects no changes in the real property tax rate between tax year
2025 and 2026. Personal Property Tax rates remain consistent with the prior tax year, but
vehicle taxes were reduced in tax year 2026 to a rate of $3.09 per $100 and are planned for
further reduction to $2.94 per 100 in tax year 2027. A full list of FY 2027 tax rates can be
found in the Revenue Chapter of the adopted budget.

Revenues and Expenditures
General Fund Revenue Budget by Source
The table below shows the adopted General Fund budget for revenues by source for fiscal
years (FY) 2020 through 2027, excluding transfers to the General Fund from other funds and
the use of prior year fund balance. As shown in the table, local revenues continue to account
for a large share of the General Fund budget – more than 96 percent in FY 2027. State
revenue accounts for 3.5 percent of the FY 2027 budget and federal revenue accounts for 0.4
percent.
Local revenues are forecasted to increase 9.1 percent in FY 2027, largely capturing better
than anticipated performance of revenues as relates to data center property. Likewise,
revenue from the Commonwealth is anticipated to increase in FY 2027 primarily due to
growth in grants and reimbursements from the Compensation Board, in addition to select tax
revenues collected by the Commonwealth and distributed to the County. Commonwealth
revenue in the General Fund does not include state funds provided directly to the Loudoun
County Public School System. Federal revenue is forecasted to decrease slightly in FY 20267
reflecting ongoing federal policy changes under the current administration.

Personal Property Taxes
The FY 2027 budget for personal property tax revenue is 5.8 percent higher than the amount
budgeted for FY 2026. This reflects the strong performance, to date, and anticipated future
performance of the data center industry and its attendant taxable computer equipment in the
County.
The chart below includes the State’s annual reimbursement to Loudoun for personal
property tax relief on personal-use motor vehicles. This reimbursement began in the FY 2001
budget as part of the planned phase out of the personal property tax on personal-use motor
vehicles. Beginning in 2006, the State imposed a limit on the phase out of the vehicle
personal property tax, capping the annual reimbursement to Loudoun at $48,070,701. The
State’s fixed-dollar reimbursement for the vehicle personal property tax has caused Loudoun
vehicle owners to realize a smaller percentage discount on their vehicle tax bill (28 percent in
calendar year 2025 but increasing to 41 percent in 2026) than is realized by residents in other
jurisdictions with slower rates of growth. The increase in TY 2026 is a product of the
significant reduction in vehicle personal property tax rates from prior tax years (down from
4.15 per $100 of valuation to 3.09).
The major contributor to the revenue annual increases shown below is data center
development, with the attendant increase in taxable computer equipment. For FY 2027, the
budget for computer equipment taxes specifically located in data centers accounts for ~77
percent of personal property tax revenue (excluding the state reimbursement), or ~$879
million. The general personal property tax rate remained at $4.20 per $100 of assessed value
between 1988 and 2022; however, in 2023 the rate was lowered to $4.15 per $100 of
1 The equalized rate is the rate that would generate the same amount of revenue in the subsequent

Personal Property Taxes

State Reimbursement

1

The State began providing a partial reimbursement for the personal property tax on personal-use
vehicles in 1999. The Personal Property Tax Reduction Act reduced the bill on the first $20,000 of
assessed value per residential vehicle by an increasing amount through 2001, when the
reimbursement rate was capped at 70 percent. The County continues to collect 100 percent of the
personal property tax on the assessed value of a vehicle that is above $20,000. Through calendar year
2005, the State reimbursed the County for the revenue lost by the 70 percent personal property tax
reduction. The 2004 State General Assembly set a fixed dollar limit on the total reimbursement
provided to localities beginning in 2006.

Real and Personal Property Taxes Per Capita1
The FY 2027 budgeted real property tax revenue per capita increased by ~$327 or 6.7
percent to $3,346. While the FY 2027 budget reflects a continuation of the tax year 2025 tax
rate of .805 per 100, this rate is 7.0 cents above the overall equalized rate (the rate that would
generate the same revenue year-over-year), and 1.0 cent above the homeowner’s equalized
rate of 0.795. The FY 2027 budgeted personal property tax revenue per capita, including the
State’s annual reimbursement for property tax relief, increased by ~$113, 4.8 percent, from
FY 2026. As shown in the chart below, personal property tax revenue per capita has grown
over the years as Loudoun has become home to more data centers. Computer equipment
taxes from data centers are the single largest source of personal property tax revenue at
approximately $879 million in FY 2027.

Charges for Services Budget and Permits, Fees, & Licenses Budget
Budgeted revenues shown on this page result from fees charged for services provided (e.g.,
after school activities, commuter bus service, solid waste disposal, etc.) and from licenses and
permits required for certain activities (e.g., land development, dog licenses, building permits,
etc.). FY 2027 revenue from charges for services is $1.55 million higher than budgeted in FY
2026, in large part from programmatic revenues tied to the County’s commuter bus
programs, in addition to increased landfill use charges. Budgeted revenue from permits,
fees, and licenses are generally on par with the FY 2026 adopted budget based on drags in
the development environment from the heightened interest rate environment, which remains
elevated above pandemic era levels despite some easing on rates by the Federal Reserve,
and based on heightened economic uncertainty.

County Government and Schools Operating Budget1
The County Government’s General Fund operating budget for FY 2027 is 7.7 percent higher
than FY 2026, while the operating budget for Loudoun County Public Schools (LCPS)
increased by 5.3 percent. For the period from FY 2018 through FY 2027 (a ten-year period),
the County Government’s General Fund operating budget increased at an average annual
rate of 9.2 percent while the operating budget for LCPS increased at an average annual rate
of 7.2 percent. Over the 10-year period, both budgets grew between 47-55 percent.

Loudoun County Public School Student Enrollment
Public school enrollment increased steadily before seemingly peaking in FY 2020 just prior to
the pandemic. Since the pandemic, enrollment has fluctuated at levels below the peak
achieved prior to the pandemic. In FY 2026, actual enrollment was 3,658 fewer students than
in FY 2020 (pre-pandemic). Student enrollment is projected to decrease 0.4 percent in FY
2027, which is negative as compared to the five-year average of 2.8 percent growth prepandemic. Student enrollment figures are reported as of September 30th of the fiscal year
(e.g., September 30, 2025 for FY 2026).

Fiscal Reserve and Unassigned General Fund
Balance
In FY 1994, the Board established the County’s fiscal reserve and adopted a policy that the
General Fund Balance designed as “committed” will always be maintained at a minimum of
10 percent of operating revenues in the General Fund1 and School Funds. The fiscal reserve
is the largest component of Committed General Fund Balance. The value of the fiscal reserve
continues to increase as County and School revenues increase. The Revenue Stabilization is a
special reserve fund established in October 2023 as a buffer specific to the County’s data
center revenues and was previously rolled into the general fiscal reserve figure reflected
below in prior budgets. It has now been called out separately as this dedicated buffer fund
grows, generally in tandem with data center real and personal property revenue (as it is
anchored to a 10 percent threshold of these two revenue streams).
Unrestricted/unassigned General Fund balance represents unspent funds in the General
Fund at the end of the fiscal year that are not reserved or designated for a specific purpose
by the Board of Supervisors. A positive fund balance occurs when actual revenue for a fiscal
year exceeds budgeted revenue or actual expenditures are less than the budgeted
expenditures (or both). Unassigned General Fund Balance for years FY 2016 through FY 2019
were in part the result of $30-45 million in positive revenue variances in business personal
property taxes (BPPT) on computer equipment. The lower value of unassigned General Fund
Balance for FY 2020 reflects the early impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic on revenues such
as recreation charges and development permits as well as a deliberate attempt to better
capture BPPT revenue from computer equipment during the budget process. The FY 2020
budget variance for BPPT revenue from computer equipment was just $7 million. Unassigned
General Fund Balance for FY 2023 was driven by strong performance in both the real and
personal property portfolios likely reflective of over performance of the data center industry
in the County, in addition to lingering vehicle-market inflationary factors playing out in
related personal property taxes. For FY 2024 and FY 2025, the Unassigned General Fund
Balance was once again principally driven by the over-performance of data center BPPT
revenue.

Fiscal Reserve and Unassigned General Fund Balance2
1 Operating revenue for the General Fund excludes one-time revenue from the sale of County assets, if

any, during a fiscal year. Operating revenue for a fiscal year appears as Total Revenue in the General
category in Exhibit V of the Annual Comprehensive Financial Report for that year. The Annual
Comprehensive Financial Report may be accessed at https://www.loudoun.gov/1476/AnnualComprehensive-Financial-Reports.
2 The Revenue Stabilization Fund is a newer reserve account created by the County in recent fiscal
years as a specific buffer for volatility as relates to data center-derived revenues.
